item.title: A major political test. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The standoff over the appointment of the vice-chancellor (VC) of Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) has become more than an administrative dispute. It raises serious questions about the authority of university administrations, the dignity of academics, the limits of student protest, and the present government’s ability to implement its decisions.
If a VC is prevented from entering his workplace for weeks, and if reports that his electricity and water connections were cut are substantiated, the matter goes beyond ordinary campus dissent.
A university cannot function properly if administrative decisions are challenged through prolonged blockades rather than transparent institutional procedures.
The allegations deserve scrutiny, and the university community deserves a clear account of what has happened.
Dr Sheikh Shariful Islam was appointed VC by an order issued in the name of the president and went to CUET to assume his responsibilities. He is also a former student of the university. His appointment can be questioned, and students have every right to demand transparency.
However, if there are specific allegations against him, they should be made public and examined through appropriate procedures. Preventing an administrator from entering his workplace is not a substitute for evidence, due process, or accountability.
One of the most striking aspects of the controversy is that the previous VC, Dr Sayem, whose reinstatement is reportedly being demanded by protesters, was also appointed by the BNP government.
Why, then, is one appointment accepted while the other has triggered such prolonged resistance?
The difference may have an explanation, but it should be stated clearly and supported by evidence.
If the objection concerns administrative performance, protesters should identify the specific failures. If it concerns irregularities in the appointment process, evidence should be presented.
If the dispute is rooted in political affiliations or rival interests on campus, that too should be examined openly. Questions have been raised about the former VC’s political associations and alleged closeness to a particular political group.
Such claims should be investigated impartially, not treated as established facts. The same standards must apply to both the former and current administrations.
There is also a broader concern: Whether any political group is using the banner of ordinary students to advance its own interests.
That is a legitimate question in a politically-contested campus environment, but it cannot be answered by speculation or labels. Credible evidence is needed.
Student movements can be genuine expressions of grievance while also being vulnerable to political influence. Recognizing that possibility should lead to scrutiny, not assumptions about every participant.
The reported length of the standoff raises another difficult question. Why has a VC who reportedly served for only 56 days become the focus of such an intense confrontation?
What specific grievances have made a prolonged blockade necessary, and why have those grievances not been resolved through a transparent process?
The number of days served does not, by itself, prove that the protest is unjustified. It does, however, make a clear explanation of the dispute all the more important.
The government should not dismiss student concerns simply because an appointment was made under its authority. Nor should it allow pressure alone to determine whether an appointed official can perform his duties.
These principles are compatible: Investigate credible complaints, publish findings where appropriate, protect peaceful protest, and ensure that campus administration can function under established rules.
This is why CUET has become a political test for the government. If prolonged blockades are allowed to become an effective way of forcing administrative decisions, similar confrontations could emerge at other public universities.
The risk is not that every campus will repeat the same events, but that groups elsewhere may conclude that sustained pressure is more effective than formal complaints and institutional procedures.
The government’s responsibility is therefore twofold. It must provide students with a fair and credible channel to raise concerns, while also protecting the right of university officials to carry out their lawful responsibilities.
If the appointment process was flawed, the government should address that through the proper process. If allegations against the VC are not substantiated, it should explain why the appointment stands and take lawful steps to restore normal university operations. Neither force without scrutiny nor concession without evidence will resolve the underlying problem.
Universities should not be controlled by any political party, and no administration should be immune from criticism. But neither should a group be able to claim a veto over institutional decisions by keeping a campus in deadlock.
Academic freedom includes the freedom to question authority; it also depends on rules that protect students, teachers, and administrators from coercion.
The CUET controversy is about more than one appointment. It asks whether public universities in Bangladesh will be governed through evidence, institutional rules, and accountability, or whether administrative decisions will increasingly be shaped by blockades and organized pressure. The government’s response will help determine which precedent is set.
A credible investigation, transparent communication, and a lawful resolution are the way forward. The government must demonstrate that it can uphold institutional rules without suppressing legitimate dissent.
That is the real test. Not whether the government can win a confrontation, but whether it can ensure that universities remain places where disputes are resolved through evidence and due process rather than intimidation.
SK Arman Hossain is a policy analyst and a graduate student of public policy at the University of Erfurt, Germany. Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Maaz Sadaqat sets sights on 2027 World Cup after ODI snub. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Maaz Sadaqat may have missed out on selection for Pakistan’s upcoming One-day International (ODI) tri-series featuring England and Sri Lanka, but the swashbuckling left-hander has his sights firmly set on next year’s World Cup.

The 21-year-old made a strong impression on the international stage in the recently concluded three-match T20I series against Sri Lanka, scoring consecutive half-centuries in the first two matches to help Pakistan clinch the series.

His performances were more than just individual milestones, signalling a shift towards a more aggressive batting approach in T20 cricket, with Maaz emerging as a key figure in the change.

He scored 50 off 29 balls in the opening match, helping Pakistan recover from an underwhelming powerplay alongside captain Sahibzada Farhan.

In the second T20I, Maaz took the attack to the Sri Lankan bowlers, smashing 96 off 51 balls, including seven sixes and six fours, to come close to a maiden international century.

His impressive run, however, will have to wait for another opportunity to continue in Pakistan colours, with the batter left out of the ODI squad despite having featured in six matches in the format, including his debut, earlier this year.

Maaz had made an immediate impact in only his second ODI against Bangladesh, scoring 75 and taking three wickets with his left-arm spin. However, he struggled to maintain that form in the subsequent home series against Australia in May-June, managing scores of eight, zero and 27 on difficult surfaces.

The reasons behind his omission from the squad for the upcoming tri-series remain unclear. The break, however, offers him an opportunity to refine his game with the 2027 World Cup in mind.

“I am targeting the ODI World Cup and I am preparing for it,” Maaz said in a video interview released by the Pakistan Cricket Board on Thursday. “I have a 15-20-day window coming up which I am going to dedicate to working on myself for the World Cup.”

The youngster, who rose from tape-ball cricket in Peshawar to become a franchise T20 sensation, has continued to build his reputation on the domestic and international circuits. He also struck two centuries in the recently concluded Caribbean Premier League season.

Maaz believes the key to his progress lies in strengthening his natural game rather than focusing excessively on his weaknesses.

“[In training] I try to work as much as I can on my strengths and less on my weaknesses, because if the ball is out of my range, I’d still be able to push it for a single or two,” he said. “However, if it is in my range, then I can hit it for six with my eyes closed.

“If you watch both my CPL and international knocks, I keep a positive intent from the very start.

“And if the ball comes in my range then I don’t spare it. And when a ball is a bit here or there, I try to rotate the strike.”

That clarity of approach also extends to his preferred batting position. Although Maaz has previously said he is open to batting anywhere in the order, he admits he is most comfortable opening the innings.

“I feel the most comfortable playing as an opener,” he said.

A place in Pakistan’s squad for the 2027 World Cup would put Maaz in contention for an opening slot alongside Saim Ayub, who is averaging nearly 47, and experienced campaigner Fakhar Zaman.

Maaz, however, views the competition for places as a challenge rather than a setback.

“Even if I am asked to bat lower in the order, I’ll try to bat so well that they [team management] are forced to push me higher,” he said.

Windies' Hope worried about excess baggage after landing another Player of the Match award. [ dawn ]
item.description:
West Indies captain Shai Hope is worried he may have to fork out excess baggage fees after picking up his third Player of the Match award on their tour of India.

The opener’s unbeaten 102 in the fourth Twenty20 International on Wednesday set up a series-levelling win in Hyderabad. He also smashed a century in the second T20 in Ranchi.

Hope has been in sizzling form throughout the tour, hitting two hundreds in the earlier One-Day International leg. And while he was pleased with his performances he said he was struggling to fit his awards in his luggage.

“To be honest, they are a bit heavy, and we have got to look at the luggage weight,” he quipped after West Indies prevailed by 24 runs.

“I think we are going to have some problems going back home.” Hope said getting off to a good start in Hyderabad was key.

“We got 50-plus opening partnership,” he added. “So it was good for us to start innings and then obviously we got that foundation, you can express yourself a bit more in the middle period and then try to give the team the best finish as could as possible.” Hope clobbered nine sixes in his 50-ball knock and drew the admiration of his opponents.

“We need to respect what he has been doing,” India opener Sanju Samson said. “He has been playing some really good cricketing shots, not taking that much risk, and respecting the bowlers as well.” Hope will look to give himself more baggage problems in Saturday’s series decider in Bengaluru.

West Indies will next visit Bangladesh for a two-test series later this month. The hosts will breathe easier knowing Hope is being rested ahead of ODI World Cup qualifiers in February.

item.title: Addressing our plastic crisis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s decision to launch a national platform to tackle plastic pollution is a welcome step towards addressing one of the country’s most persistent environmental challenges.
However, its success will depend on whether we see real commitment to concrete action rather than it becoming another initiative that produces discussions without meaningful results.
Plastic pollution has become an increasingly visible threat across Bangladesh, with plastic waste continuing to damage ecosystems and threaten public health. Excessive reliance on single-use plastics, poor waste management, and inadequate recycling facilities have allowed the problem to grow.
The consequences affect everyone -- particularly communities whose livelihoods depend on healthy waterways and a clean environment.
Bringing together government agencies, businesses, development partners, and civil society can therefore help improve coordination and promote a circular economy.
However, consumers cannot be expected to shoulder the responsibility alone. Manufacturers, importers, and brand owners must also be held accountable for the waste generated by their products.
The government must establish clear targets for reducing plastic use, expanding recycling, and improving waste collection. Existing regulations must be enforced consistently, with meaningful penalties for non-compliance. Businesses should be encouraged to reduce unnecessary packaging and invest in reusable alternatives.
Without effective monitoring, even well-intentioned policies will struggle to deliver lasting change.
Waste collectors, sorters and recyclers also have a role to play. Many work in unsafe conditions without adequate protection or recognition, and improving their working conditions and integrating them into formal waste management systems would strengthen the country’s recycling capacity.
Public awareness must be prioritized, along with adequate collection facilities and stronger enforcement. Local authorities need sufficient resources to manage waste effectively, while households and businesses must have accessible disposal options.
This platform presents an opportunity to coordinate efforts and establish accountability across sectors. Its success must include reduced plastic waste, higher recycling rates, and cleaner rivers and neighbourhoods.
Bangladesh cannot afford another initiative that exists only on paper.

item.title: Rural women have shaped our country. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The International Day of Rural Women, observed today, is an opportunity to recognize the contributions of women to rural communities -- especially in Bangladesh, where recognition remains far removed from their lived reality.
Despite their contributions to agriculture, household economies, and community life, rural women continue to be marginalized, with limited access to resources, opportunities, and decision-making.
Women play a significant role in Bangladesh’s agricultural sector -- yet female farmers often remain invisible in a system that frequently acknowledges men as the primary agricultural workers. Their labour is undervalued, and many lack ownership of the land they cultivate.
Without land titles, access to institutional credit, quality seeds, modern equipment, and agricultural training, they are left at a disadvantage despite their essential contributions to food security.
This inequality extends beyond farming: Rural women often face barriers to education, healthcare, formal employment, and financial services.
For women in climate-vulnerable areas, floods, cyclones, and river erosion add another layer of insecurity, threatening livelihoods and increasing the burden of keeping families afloat.
Addressing these challenges requires more than celebrating women once a year. Female farmers must be formally recognized in agricultural policies and included in training programs, subsidies, and credit schemes.
Ensuring women's access to land ownership and inheritance rights is equally important. Local government institutions must also create opportunities for rural women to participate meaningfully in decisions that affect their lives.
Furthermore, investments in rural education, healthcare, childcare, and safe employment can help women move beyond economic dependence. Support for women-led cooperatives and small businesses would also help create sustainable livelihoods.
Bangladesh cannot achieve inclusive development while a substantial part of its rural workforce remains overlooked. Rural women are active contributors to our economic development, and their labour must be valued, their rights protected, and their voices heard.
The true measure of this day will be whether recognition translates into lasting changes in their everyday lives.

item.title: Inside the collapse of education in the Rohingya camps. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Abdur Rashid keeps returning to the same subtraction.
He teaches at a learning centre inside Kutupalong Registered Camp , the settlement where he grew up after his family fled Myanmar, and the number he cannot make work is his own paycheck.
“I am not earning any fixed amount of salary from this community-led school. My earnings depend on the payment possible to gather from different families in this camp,” Rashid says.
“If I could teach at any learning centres under a donor-funded learning program, I might earn a stipend of around Tk 13,000 for teaching as a volunteer,” he said, describing the opportunity he lost.
Many Rohingya teachers like him have had to face this reality in Cox’s Bazar since 2025.
Rashid finished his primary schooling in camp, then pushed through years of paperwork and travel restrictions to earn a bachelor’s degree from local colleges in Cox’s Bazar.
Now, he is managing a community-led school that Rohingya families increasingly treat as their only dependable option.
He is careful not to call this progress.
“When formal donor funding began to falter, educated community members stepped forward to keep our children learning,” he says.
“That stepping-in comes at a cost that families absorb directly, rather than through an aid budget.”
Families in his network pay roughly $0.50 to $6.50 a month to keep whiteboards, markers, and modest teacher stipends flowing.
It is a system built out of necessity rather than design, and Rashid is one of thousands of Rohingya educators now holding it together by hand.
A system built for emergency, not permanence
When more than 730,000 Rohingya fled Myanmar’s Rakhine State in 2017, aid agencies opened temporary learning centres within months, teaching basic literacy in Burmese, English, and math.
Initially, children were taught using an informal curriculum called the Learning Competency Framework and Approach (LCFA).
This curriculum attempted to include Burmese, English, and Mathematics; many teachers recruited from the host community were entirely unequipped to teach in Burmese.
The curriculum failed to reconcile the spoken Rohingya dialect with Burmese written script, creating severe comprehension barriers for children.
Later on, the Bangladesh government and Unicef launched a Myanmar Curriculum by late 2021, expanding coverage toward all 410,000 school-age children in the camps through 3,200 learning centres.
A record 300,000 children enrolled in school in 2023-24, the first time Rohingya children of all ages were studied under one standardized curriculum. A dedicated campaign pulled 13,000 out-of-school children into classrooms.
However, this learning framework, temporary by design, was meant not to function as a real school network.
Host-community and Rohingya teachers taught children only five subjects through instruction in Burmese and English.
They progressed automatically through grades without formal examinations.
When the money stopped
The arithmetic Rashid does every month became the arithmetic of the entire humanitarian sector in June 2025.
The $300 million USAid fund in 2024 had fallen to $12m in June 2025.
By April, the humanitarian education sector had secured only $22m of its required $72m.
The cutbacks affected more than 6,400 learning centres across 33 camps, home to over 1.2 million people, pushing roughly 300,000 of the camps’ 437,000 school-age children out of classrooms.
Around 1,250 teachers lost their jobs overnight when Unicef and Save the Children suspended all donor-funded learning programs.
“When funds from major bilateral donors are reduced overnight, agencies face excruciating trade-offs. You cannot strip a family of their minimum 1,900-calorie daily food ration or shut down cholera treatment facilities.”
A knowledge management officer with Unicef Bangladesh in Cox’s Bazar, speaking confidentially, explained the rationale plainly.
“Education, while vital for long-term human development, is treated as a secondary priority during acute budget shortfalls.”
The community steps in
What replaced the closed centres was not a plan. It was families like the ones Rashid works with. They quietly rebuilt a parallel system out of tuition fees and volunteer labour.
These community-run schools now operate on something close to a private micro-school model, staffed by educators who completed their own upper-secondary schooling and teach one subject at a time.
The clearest sign that this parallel system now sees itself as permanent came in March 2026, when the newly formed Examination Board of Rohingya Refugees held its first matriculation exams, with question papers handed to Bangladesh’s Armed Police Battalion for secure delivery across camp exam centres.
Fifty three community-run schools joined the board at its founding, and the network now covers kindergarten through grade twelve with free enrolment.
It offers something the old learning centres never could: A certificate a student can actually hold onto.
A script they were never taught
Rohingya children in Myanmar were denied both Burmese literacy and any formal way to write their own language for decades.
Even a decade ago, aid workers were warning that most children were adopting Bengali instead , simply because it was more useful day-to-day than their mother tongue.
That changed in 2024, when Children on the Edge, a child rights organization, piloted mother-tongue lessons in Hanifi script across its Kutupalong and Bhasan Char classrooms, training more than 70 teachers for a program that now reaches over 6,300 children .
The Hanifi Rohingya script, developed in the 1980s and added to the Unicode standard in 2018, gave the language a modern, typeable form for the first time; it took years before any classroom actually taught it.
Even so, the shift remains marginal in light of the crisis; nearly 50 community schools teach the script at all, and most learning centres and madrasas still default to Burmese or Bengali, the languages of the systems around them rather than the language of the children inside them.
Where the mosque becomes the classroom
Many parents have expressed frustration with donor-funded learning centres, as they focus heavily on play-based learning and basic alphabet skills without offering a clear path to high school.
Parents in refugee camps prefer madrasas over donor-funded learning centres due to deep-seated cultural, structural, and operational differences. They worry that temporary frameworks will dilute traditional community values.
Religious learning in madrasas has deep roots in Rohingya communities that predate the 2017 exodus, and the camps’ network, running through neighbourhood maktabs and a formal examining body called Wifaq al-Madaris al-Arabia al-Rohingiya , has expanded quietly through years when donor-funded classrooms were closing.
Unlike the learning centres, madrasas generally do not require birth registration or other legal documentation many refugee families lack, and they are funded privately, often by donors in Saudi Arabia and Turkey rather than through the camps’ formal humanitarian architecture.
An education sector specialist who is sceptical of madrasas as a systemic fix concedes the pull is genuine.
“Madrasas are deeply embedded in the cultural landscape, but they cannot serve as a structural replacement for formal education,” the specialist said.
“They lack a standardized curriculum, formal learning outcome assessments, and recognized pathways toward higher education.”
As Cox’s Bazar nears a decade of hosting the mass influx of Rohingya refugees, the prolonged decay of primary education threatens not only the immediate welfare of children but the future stability of the entire region.
The existing learning framework currently provided to Rohingya children offers no viable long-term future.
Without funding commitment, the half-built futures of Rohingya children will remain permanently stalled in the muddy hills of Cox’s Bazar, leaving an entire generation stranded between a homeland they cannot return to and a world that has turned its back on their education.
Rashid does not need that document to know what adjustment and funding shifts look like from inside a classroom.
What thousands of teachers like him have built is not a fix for what donors walked away from. It is the measure of what remains in their hands.
Zulker Naeen is a Research Coordinator, Centre for Critical and Qualitative Studies (CQS) and Adjunct Faculty, Department of Media Studies and Journalism (MSJ), University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB). item.title: Is AI the ultimate solution?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In today’s world of the internet, social media, and various streaming platforms, our daily lives have fully submitted to technology. It’s not been too long ago that we were introduced to the internet, and today, most if not all of us are using it every day.
Recently, there have been a lot of AI trends and challenges going viral, where the user needs to upload a photo on ChatGPT to get a modified and edited photo. They share these photos on social media for the sole purpose of “fun.” However, the aftermath of that one picture is more than one can imagine.
To talk about the effects of using AI will be a long conversation with plenty of controversial and political agendas. With increased use of AI, we, as its users, are only providing more data to the big tech companies like Google and Meta who benefit with every click, every upload, and every engagement by collecting our personal information.
The individuals in authority of these personal data ultimately are invading people’s privacy and dehumanizing them by abusing their power. The collected data could be nothing but just the age of the user or their gender, but there are multiple ways this information is misused.
We know that there are various facial recognition machines being used for every sector. The data collected through these machines are processed to develop generati ve AI along with making weapons.
Another thing that helps AI and its function is algorithms. We know the word algorithm as something that helps curate our social media pages. Every ‘like’, ‘share’, or any engagement done on social media helps create data which the algorithm picks up as the user's information.
Each unique page is the result of an algorithm after understanding the user's interests through collected data. But algorithms do not only work on social media but rather, work beyond just our social media explore pages.
Every piece of information forms a code that AI tools read and gather in their system. The use of AI or any other technology is not as simple as we think.
Advanced technologies were invented with the purpose of making everyone’s daily work a bit easier. But it is important that as users, we educate ourselves with its uses, functions, and effects.
When these technologies are marketed, they are presented as tools to make our lives easier. Yet, we are never given a manual on how to use it. Furthermore, we are unaware of what they are doing after collecting our personal information.
Many use generative AI for help when they are stuck with work. Students, corporate workers, even people working in creative sectors use generative AI for their daily tasks.
But running to ChatGPT for every single task is not only dangerous, it is also damaging our ability to think creatively.
Looking back at the history of ChatGPT trends, the first one that became viral and concerning was transforming personal photos into “Ghibli style” images. People were paying for ChatGPT subscriptions only to edit their picture to look like a scene from a Ghibli movie.
This was very disappointing for the artists, animators, illustrators, and every other individual who sometimes worked for months just to draw a frame of these movies.
The Japanese animator Hayao Miyazaki expressed his disappointment, talking about how this is disrespectful to everyone working in the animation industry.
Looking at the situation now, it seems like we as a society are not educated enough to understand how much our actions are damaging our future with our AI usage.
We need to comprehend that the use of generative AI, which people use only for “fun,” has negative effects beyond what we often imagine. It is simultaneously damaging the ecological balance of the climate and harming every living being on this planet.
People should be more conscious and aware of every action, and ask questions about whether we are harming anyone or not. With our daily lives being so dependent on online platforms and services, we should not be jumping into participating in any viral trend.
It is unavoidable to use advanced technologies. However, it should not come at the expense of our ability to imagine and create.
We should always remember that AI or any technological tools are made by humans. It is us humans who program them for our use. We should not let technology take over our lives.
Let us all as a society become more aware of the functions and effects of AI, or any advanced technologies before blindly using them. The increased use of advanced technologies is not the solution to all our problems. Rather, it could be inviting the end of everything sooner than we can imagine.
Nushin Tarannum Lamia is a graduate student of Communication Culture and Media at Drexel University, Philadelphia, USA.

item.title: Achakzai warns governor's rule will next be imposed in Sindh over water, mines. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Opposition Leader in the National Assembly Mehmood Khan Achakzai warned on Wednesday that governor’s rule would be imposed next in Sindh over the “occupation of water, mines and streams”, urging the Centre to give provinces their rights and resources.

He was speaking in the National Assembly, where a resolution endorsing the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Sunday was passed. The federal government cited the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism as the reason for imposing governor’s rule in KP.

In days preceding the development, political tensions between the federal government and the opposition, mainly the PTI, had remained high after the party announced a long march to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. However, the march, initially planned for Islamabad, remained confined to KP until it fizzled out with the imposition of governor’s rule in the province.

In his address, Achakzai said KP’s “mistake is that it saved itself with the help of its people”. He also drew a comparison between the current situation with regards to KP and the one witnessed at the time of the creation of Bangladesh.

He also assailed the government for depriving the PTI of its election symbol ahead of the 2024 general elections. “And the mistake of his (Imran’s) party’s workers was that they contested the elections on 200 different symbols and turned your own game around on you. You are meting out the punishment for that? You are punishing 240 million people of Pakistan for that?”

The opposition leader also pointed that Sohail Afridi, who has become non-functional as the chief minister after the imposition of governor’s rule and had been leading the PTI’s march, had not resorted to violence or using expletives in his call for the protest.

He went on to say, “When you try to snatch our right to self-determination, our right to vote, we all will stand against you. All of us, all provinces.”

Noting the participation of the PPP, which is in power in Sindh, Achakzai said it pained him. He then warned that governor’s rule would next be imposed in Sindh over the “occupation of water, mines and streams”.

“And then you will recall your mistake.”

He said there was still time to rectify mistakes.

“Reverse these decisions,” Achakzai said, urging for making Parliament the centre of power. “And Pakistan will be saved,” he remarked.

He warned that when the “state turns against its own people, they are compelled to look elsewhere”.

The opposition also criticised the government over the country’s economy situation.

“You are looting this country’s resources […] Have some mercy on this country. […] This country is drowning because of our mistakes. There is only one way to save it: through its Constitution and Parliament and by have a democratic system,” he asserted.

Achakzai also lamented the fact the Parliament was not taken into confidence over decisions related to foreign affairs, and that Pakistan had strained ties with most of its neighbours.

On Imran, who has not been allowed meeting with his family and associates for a long time, Achakzai said: “Which provision of the Constitution … places a restriction on meetings with the most popular leader of the country?”

He assured that if meetings were arrangement with Imran, “we will just try to assess his health condition and will try to resolve matter between you. We promise we will meet him and not tell anyone. […] Have some sense. Negotiate”.

He concluded his address by declaring that the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP was wrong.

item.title: National Assembly, Senate pass resolutions endorsing Centre's imposition of emergency in KP. [ dawn ]
item.description:
ISLAMABAD: Shortly after the National Assembly passed a resolution endorsing the federal government’s imposition of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Wednesday, the Senate also gave its approval for the measure.

The Centre had imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Sunday, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The move followed weeks of political tensions between the Centre and the PTI after the latter announced a long march to Islamabad to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan.

Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry tabled the motions regarding the proclamation of emergency before both Houses.

Senate proceedings

In the Senate, the resolution was passed amid the opposition’s outcry, with PTI senators staging a walkout.

The Senate’s approval followed a heated debate between treasury and opposition members, during which Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar defended the procedural propriety presenting the resolution in the House and getting it approved.

He argued that a “constitutional resolution” had been laid before the House in accordance with the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Senate. “Under Article 232, a copy of [the proclamation of] emergency has been laid before the House. An attempt to bypass the constitutional procedure cannot succeed,” he said, adding that the requirement of a seven-day notice for tabling a resolution did not apply to one presented under a constitutional necessity.

“If its opponents have any objections, they should reject the resolution through their vote after the debate. We cannot deviate from the Constitution and rules of the House,” he said.

As opposition voiced opposition to the resolution, Senate Chairperson Yousuf Raza Gilani asked them to exercise patience. “This is not a classroom, do not make noise,” he remarked as senators from the opposition benches continued sloganeering.

Among them, PTI’s Humayun Mohmand said independent Senator Faisal Vawda had said months ago that governor’s rule would be imposed. He alleged that terrorism being cited as the reason for the measure was just an excuse and the actual “target is the PTI”.

“The decision to impose governor’s rule and emergency was taken months ago,” he alleged. Seemingly referring to the creation of Bangladesh, he said the federal government’s decision since 1970 had proved wrong.

PTI-backed Senator Hamid Khan also argued that there “seems to be some other objectives behind governor’s rule and emergency”. Referring to the talks between the Centre and the opposition ahead of governor’s rule and emergency in KP, he alleged that negotiations “were just a drama” and were held “only to deceive the people”.

“The real decision was taken elsewhere long ago,” he claimed. He further said that Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam Fazl chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, who tried to mediate between the Centre and the opposition, had stated that while the negotiations were taking place, “a decision came”.

“Governments formed on the basis of Form-47 do not have the real mandate,” he added.

He further regretted that after the 26th Amendment, “there is neither any Constitution nor an independent judicial system”.

“The judiciary has been stripped of its independence, which closes the avenues to challenge unconstitutional steps,” he said.

Khan went on to say: “Article 232 has to be presented before the House for debate, not just for saying yes. Decision was taken by those whom Constitution does not allow to take the decision, but they have complete dominance over Constitution. At this time, neither is there any Constitution nor any court in the country.”

PTI Senator Mohsin Aziz railed against federal ministers, who have been accusing the PTI of facilitating terrorism.

“You talk about terrorism, what do you know about terrorism? People of KP sacrificed their children and picked up bodies. […] Did we support Pakistan or terrorists? Those calling people of KP terrorists should be ashamed. These are valiant people who saved this country,” he said.

Aziz said terrorism was a result of unemployment, hunger, non-availability of hospitals, water and education.

Senator Zeeshan Khanzada, also from the PTI, said he condemned the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP. He accused the federal government of “abducting” Sohail Afridi, who has been rendered non-functional as the KP chief minister following the imposition of governor’s rule, and other PTI MPAs.

JUI-F’s Kamran Murtaza said the opposition’s resolution against governor’s rule should have also been included in the agenda for the day, but it was returned with objections.

Murtaza argued that the relevant material required for endorsement of enforcement of Article 232 and 234 — constitutional provision related to imposition of emergency and governor’s rule — had not been presented in the House.

Despite letters and applications, the government had not provided documents and material related to the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule, he said, adding that senators had to obtain that material through social media.

Members could not be satisfied with a decision until complete information came forth, he said.

NA proceedings

The NA question hour session was suspended due to discussions on the emergency. The motion in the lower House of Parliament was adopted with a majority vote after a discussion opened by Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar.

“The National Assembly approves the Proclamation of Emergency issued by the President on the 11th October, 2026 in the Province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under second proviso of clause (1) of Article 232 of the Constitution,” read a post by NA’s official X account.

According to Article 232, if the “president acts on his own, the Proclamation of Emergency shall be placed” before both Houses of the Parliament for approval by each House within 10 days.

Meanwhile, a proclamation for governor’s rule issued under Article 234 “shall be laid before a joint sitting and shall cease to be in force at the expiration of two months”, unless a joint sitting approves its extension. However, such a measure shall not remain in force for more than six months.

Throughout Wednesday’s proceedings, opposition members participated calmly and did not stage any loud protest, unlike past instances when the PTI objects to the Centre.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also attended part of the session, with pictures released by the NA showing him shaking hands with Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai.

Federal ministers defended the emergency imposition while assailing what they described as the PTI-led KP government’s lack of will to combat terrorism.

In tune with that, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari blamed the PTI for the circumstances that compelled the Centre to impose emergency in KP and termed it a “political suicide attack” for the party.

However, he also urged the treasury and the opposition to get back on the path of dialogue and make joint efforts against terrorism.

At one point during the proceedings, NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq noted that the Oct 3 dialogue was held in a cordial atmosphere.

Sadiq praised both sides for “attempting more than their capacity so that the matter is settled”.

However, he said some matters were beyond the parties’ control and voiced his support for forming the same committees for negotiations if ever needed in the future.

Addressing PTI lawmakers, the speaker said, “Everyone’s response was that this [process of dialogue] should continue, but you also understand that your hands were tied.”

He took note of the PTI’s complaints regarding the jail conditions of party founder Imran Khan, adding that he had even provided details of facilities provided to the jailed ex-premier.

The session was adjourned to meet again at 11am on Oct 16 (Friday).

‘Political suicide attack’

Bilawal began his speech by highlighting that emergency and governor’s rule in KP were measures taken under the Constitution. Reading the relevant provisions, he asserted that the Centre tried its best to “engage the opposition so this step did not have to be taken”.

“They will have to accept, even if not publicly, but the responsible leadership of the opposition knows that the PTI itself carried out a political suicide attack on its KP government,” he remarked.

The PPP chief maintained that the PTI could not deny that its “leadership, particularly in the province had a key role in the political, constitutional and legal circumstances” at present.

Bilawal emphasised that the PPP’s stance was that “before employing this constitutional atomic bomb, we must engage with PTI and the opposition and try to address the federal government’s reservations that they were not supporting them in the war against terrorism”.

He observed: “If political space is restricted for one political party, it is impossible that it remains restricted for that particular party; it is limited for every political party, political worker and Pakistani citizen.

“We are responsible for this, but you cannot deny that you are also responsible for it,” he said.

Terming the imposition of emergency a “difficult decision”, Bilawal recalled alleged remarks by Sohail Afridi — the KP chief minister whose role is now non-functional — that he would not combat terrorism the way the Centre wanted.

“If this was not a political suicide, then what else was it?”

The Bhutto scion wondered if the opposition and Afridi had left any reason for President Asif Ali Zardari, who he said prides himself on passing the 18th Amendment, to “refuse to sign” the emergency proclamation.

He argued that due to the PTI’s actions and statements, neither the president, the Centre, nor he had any legal or political reason left for not imposing emergency in KP.

“But even today, I would recommend to the federal government that we extend our hand forward once again for negotiations, political discussions and try to find a resolution and a middle path,” Bilawal added.

The PPP chairman noted that emergency was “always a stopgap measure”.

“We cannot sustain the emergency forever,” he added, emphasising that while the counterterrorism fight would be better than before, an “all-of-society and all-of-country response” was needed to eradicate it completely.

Regarding the Oct 3 talks of a joint delegation of the PPP and the government with the opposition, Bilawal said, “Late at night, I was informed that congratulations, negotiations are succeeding.”

He said the PTI was willing to declare the areas in KP with surging terrorism as “terrorist areas”, and the opposition was about to agree that the federal and KP governments would sign a pact on joint efforts against terrorism. However, the dialogue collapsed.

The former foreign minister pointed out that the security challenges Pakistan was facing were “way more complicated” than before, adding that India “could still not digest […] its embarrassment” from the May 2025 conflict.

Referring to remarks by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi that its ‘Operation Sindoor’ was still ongoing, Bilawal said: “It means that India is still sponsoring terrorist incidents in Pakistan, sometimes in the form of TTP (Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan) and sometimes in the form of separatist terrorist groups.”

He reiterated Pakistan’s stance that India was involved in terrorist activities being conducted from across the Afghan border.

The ex-foreign minister then highlighted Islamabad’s role as a mediator in the US-Iran war.

“But there is a state — which we do not recognise as a state — that will neither be happy nor ever forget that you took this step. And those Zionist forces will and are interfering in Pakistan’s internal politics and state.”

Concluding his speech, the PPP chairman emphasised the need for building consensus on “some fundamental issues” for an empowered lower house.

“Even today, we are saying, come and at least begin from this house,” he said while addressing the opposition benches.

Gohar demands implementation of NAP

Speaking in the NA, PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan said his party “rejected” the Centre’s move to impose emergency in KP.

He asked what “terrorism” Imran’s wife or sisters had allegedly been involved in that they had been put behind bars, or what the accusations were against the PTI MNAs and MPAs who he said were detained.

Gohar further said, “One person is not present in the house currently. When he comes during a joint session, then I will reveal the reality of the negotiations.”

He affirmed that the PTI had raised its voice against terrorism, adding that measures against the scourge must be taken according to the National Action Plan (NAP).

Gohar argued that the PML-N opposition during the PTI’s tenure carried out “14 long marches in two years, but you did not let us stage even one long march”.

Presenting his version of the Oct 3 talks with the government, the PTI leader said his party was being asked to immediately call off the long march. “I said where did [the topic] of terrorism arise from suddenly.”

Noting that the government had put forward “five reservations”, Gohar said PTI was willing to make the KP Police Act similar to that of Punjab and Sindh.

The PTI leader reiterated his party’s request for the production of certain MNAs it says were taken into custody.

Gohar also welcomed Bilawal’s proposal to continue dialogue.

Responding to Gohar’s remarks, the PPP chairman said the PTI was busy in its long march while the people of KP were being targeted by terrorists.

Bilawal reiterated that the opposition could keep arguing against the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, but no one could deny that the decision was grounded in the Constitution.

“I cannot insist on the government to continue talks with PTI despite being defrauded multiple times,” the PPP chairman said.

Pointing towards Gohar and Achakzai, Bilawal said: “I believe that none of them is allied with terrorists. I believe that they will definitely want to combat terrorism; however, they cannot deny the fact that their former chief minister contradicted this fact.”

Bilawal again requested all the stakeholders to unite and combat terrorism collectively. He also called for the provision of all facilities to the incarcerated PTI founder.

‘Threat to national security’

Addressing the house, the law minister explained that emergency was imposed in KP as the security situation there was becoming a threat to “national security”.

Tarar noted that after the Proclamation of Emergency was issued, the Constitution’s Article 232 required that both houses of the parliament approve the measure.

He recalled that the federal cabinet examined “material” regarding terrorism in the province during its Oct 11 meeting and then advised PM Shehbaz to recommend the imposition of emergency.

He noted that some people compared the measure to the emergency imposed by former dictator Gen Pervez Musharraf on Oct 12, 1999.

The minister particularly noted “internal disturbances” and cross-border infiltrations. He contended that the situation since Oct 15, 2025, when Sohail Afridi’s government came into power in KP, was “turning into a threat to national security to an alarming extent”.

He went on to highlight that there was a rise in terrorism in KP, especially after 2021, due to the approach of the provincial government.

“Perhaps there might be foreign, diplomatic and political reasons behind it, which got inflamed due to a political party’s point of view.”

Tarar stated that 2,911 incidents of terrorism took place between 2021 and 2024 in KP, but they surged to 3,787 incidents between Oct 15, 2025 and Oct 9, 2026.

He criticised the KP chief minister for ignoring martyred security and police personnel, and for instead preferring to promote his political designs and make visits across the country.

“Even this was announced that the federal capital will be conquered,” he said, referring to the party’s plan to hold a protest long march towards the federal capital.

The PML-N leader expressed his government’s gratitude to NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq for providing a platform for dialogue between the Centre and the opposition. He reiterated the government’s stance that the PTI had the agreement draft changed multiple times, but even then backed off from it.

Tarar observed that the PTI demanded the release of their party founder Imran Khan and his treatment in a private hospital despite knowing that only courts could provide such a relief.

He said two days would be “remembered in the country’s democratic history with regard to misfortune and a political party”.

On the emergency measure, the law minister noted that a special mechanism has been introduced for 12 districts of KP.

Speaking after Tarar, Achakzai criticised him for trying to prove that terrorism was not tackled in KP.

The opposition leader questioned the government’s mandate in the February 2024 general elections, quipping that the opposition would “surrender” if the minister could swear that the government won those polls fairly.

Achakzai alleged that the incumbent ruling coalition was formed “illegally”.

‘You do not have clean hands’

Meanwhile, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif went on to recall the tenure of the PTI government in the Centre and assailed the party’s past actions.

Referring to ex-prime minister Imran Khan’s plan to resettle members of the TTP, he said PTI tried to convince the then-opposition that “bringing these terrorists back would be better for Pakistan”.

The PML-N leader mentioned the 2019 episode of an Indian pilot’s capture in Pakistan: “They had threatened and we were surrendering. The then-prime minister was saying, ‘What should I do? Attack India?’”

Asif urged the opposition to reflect on its past actions, adding that Imran often used to praise former army chief retired General Qamar Javed Bajwa.

“As long as this contradiction remains in our words and actions and in our society, the circumstances of this country will not fix.”

He narrated his time behind bars during the PTI government, when Shehbaz “smuggled a blanket” to him to brace the low temperatures. “I used to eat the jail’s food,” he said, claiming that orders were given to remove the geyser when it was installed.

“But we did not hold rallies or mourn at D-Chowk or dig graves. We did not martyr police and law enforcement personnel,” Asif remarked.

“You demand equity when you have clean hands. You do not have clean hands, you cannot demand equity; this is a thousand-year-old principle,” he contended.

“You know very well what Gen Musharraf did to me. There was a 4x6 cell in Attock jail,” the PML-N politician said, emphasising that he stood with his party and ex-PM Nawaz Sharif.

Speaking on the current political situation, Asif alleged that Afridi used to “take directives […] from a person sitting in Afghanistan”.

He referred to a statement by the TTP condemning the imposition of emergency and deployment of troops in certain places. “Who is their ally and who is their rival?” he said.

The minister further countered the PTI’s stance that its leaders have not been able to meet Imran, who is imprisoned in the Adiala jail. “Meetings are held, [but] a lot of them are not publicised or brought on record,” he maintained.

Farooq Sattar urges PTI to ‘openly condemn terrorism’

In his remarks on the floor of the lower house, Farooq Sattar expressed Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan’s (MQM-P) confidence in the decision taken by the prime minister.

“This was an extremely difficult decision, but so unavoidable that you had no other option,” Sattar said about imposing emergency and governor’s rule.

“We trust your decision as we trust your experience, capabilities, political acumen, and that you made this decision in the interest of the nation,” he added.

The MQM-P lawmaker contended that the PTI was “on the wrong side and does not have concrete arguments” to declare that the decision was baseless or made with political motives.

“The main issue is of the mindset,” he declared, adding that Imran had “publicly said that the war on terror is not ours”. “This is their policy. This is their mindset.”

Sattar questioned whether the KP government had ever published reports to expose terrorist hideouts and extremist trends. He further raised questions about the government’s pursuit of cases against suspected terrorists.

“Openly condemn terrorism; else, the allegation of backing [it], if a commission is formed and God forbid, it is proven in the inquiry that there is political extremism and terrorism complicity, there is a nexus, then where will you go?”

Sattar recounted his past MQM experiences, saying, “I have also suffered such times. A lot of times, the narrative coming from the top was difficult to defend. Today, I feel that Barrister Gohar is also not in the position to defend his [party’s] position on KP.”

item.title: Fire safety remains a distant dream. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The 12-hour blaze that engulfed Chawkbazar markets is yet another horrific reminder of Dhaka’s woeful preparedness for fires, especially congested areas such as Old Dhaka.
Once again, firefighters battled not just flames, but choked alleys, absence of nearby water sources, and warehouses packed with volatile plastics and chemicals.
At this stage, the tragedy no longer lies in the unpredictability of the blaze, but in its utter inevitability.
For years now, investigation committees have churned out expert recommendations to secure Old Dhaka -- clear, actionable mandates. From relocating an estimated 25,000 hazardous chemical units to designated industrial estates to enforcing building safety codes to installing street-level fire hydrants to unblocking emergency exits to increasing general awareness among the citizens.
Yet, these lifesaving measures remain almost entirely ignored, gathering dust while municipal authorities default to bureaucratic inertia.
This persistent negligence is a national shame. Short-term eviction drives launched after major tragedies are routinely suspended and abandoned under pressure from business syndicates, while long-promised chemical industrial zones languish in administrative limbo.
Allowing these unlicensed, highly flammable stockpiles to exist side-by-side with sleeping families is a criminal gamble with human lives, and how we continue to normalize this defies belief.
There is no reason for the present government to allow such callous inertia. We must break this fatal cycle of post-disaster posturing and long-term inaction.
Pledges and sympathy visits to fire sites will not extinguish chemical fires. What is urgently required is an unyielding, zero-tolerance enforcement campaign, and holding those accountable for endangering lives for the sake of profit. Enough is enough.

item.title: Campus politics must give way to reason. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is safe to say that at this point, the deepening crisis at the Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) with regard to the new vice-chancellor (VC) has reached an alarming and unacceptable threshold.
With classes and administrative functions paralyzed as a result of prolonged student blockades, and faculty and staff declaring total non-cooperation, the situation has devolved into chaos -- one that is hurting not just education for the students of the university, but also calls to attention the politicization of our higher education institutions.
Universities are meant to be beacons of rational discourse and intellectual pursuit, not battlegrounds for toxic partisan confrontation. Unfortunately, this is something our country has consistently failed to realize, and we are disappointed that the current situation is following suit.
That the VC position in our universities has remained so politicized is nothing if not an abject failure that has hurt education in this country. Even for the present situation, entering the university flanked by political cadres and forcing entry past padlocked gates is not the conduct expected of an academic leader.
Such heavy-handed optics bear an uncomfortable resemblance to the authoritarian administrative tactics of past eras, alienating the campus community and hardening student resistance.
However, we need cooler heads to prevail and move on from this. The ongoing shutdown is adversely affecting the student body at large, disrupting academic calendars and increasing anxiety for thousands of students. Shutting the VC for hours in his office and rejecting institutional channels altogether will not resolve the underlying dispute nor bring about a productive outcome.
A solution needs to be reached, and it demands immediate, serious intervention from the government who can no longer afford to remain passive observers.
There is a chasm that needs to be bridged; CUET cannot be allowed to remain held hostage, nor can disputes and disagreements be normalized in our universities and allowed to adversely affect the future of all other students.

item.title: Afghanistan produce thrilling rearguard to save Bangladesh Test. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Sediqullah Atal’s marathon century and some inspired lower-order resistance inspired Afghanistan to a dramatic draw in the one-off Test against Bangladesh on Tuesday.

Opener Atal, playing only his third Test, batted for eight-and-a-half hours for his 332-ball 111 before number nine Qais Ahmad hit an unbeaten 49 in Abu Dhabi.

Having started the final day on 132-3, Afghanistan survived to finish on 346-8, from a total of 142 overs, after being set a nominal 479-run target to win.

When Atal fell to a close-in catch off left-arm spinner Taijul Islam soon after tea with the score at 281-7, Bangladesh were in sight of victory.

But Qais and fellow tail-ender Yamin Ahmadzai (19 off 85 balls) batted for 110 deliveries in a valiant 45-run stand for the eighth wicket to resist Bangladesh’s spinners.

Even when Ahmadzai fell to Mehidy Hasan Miraz, Bangladesh had five overs to enforce a win but Qais and number 10 Zia-ur-Rehman hung on, although not without drama.

There were two missed run-out chances in the final session and a dropped catch, while Qais gave his team-mates watching from the boundary some heart-stopping moments.

The leg-spinner mixed solid defence with a penchant for dancing down the pitch, even hitting the second ball of the last over for six.

The Bangladesh players were less than impressed with Qais when he went down with an apparent hamstring injury and received treatment after playing a forward defence with 10 minutes remaining.

With a famous draw already secured, he hammered the final delivery of the match deep over midwicket for another maximum, falling to the turf in celebration.

Pacer Ebadot Hossain took 3-50 and off-spinner Miraz finished with 3-73, but it was not enough for Bangladesh.

Bangladesh skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto praised Afghanistan’s resilience.

“It is disappointing not win, but Afghanistan played brilliantly,” said Shanto. “I expected the spinners to come into the match. They tried but Afghanistan played very good cricket.”

Sediqullah earlier reached his century with a boundary off Hasan Mahmud, becoming the first Afghanistan batter to reach three figures in the fourth innings of a Test.

Hashmatullah Shahidi also scored 36 and helped Atal defy the Bangladesh bowling, but holed out to mid-on attempting a big shot down the ground, just seven minutes before tea.

Ismat Alam batted for 60 deliveries for his four — scoring his first run off his 44th delivery — before Miraz had him caught by Shanto.

With under two hours left, Bangladesh were finally rewarded with Sediqullah’s wicket as the left-hander pushed a turning delivery from Islam and a thick edge was well caught at short-leg by Tanzid Hasan.

But the exploits of Ahmadzai, Qais and Zia ensured the Afghans had the last say.

item.title: Maaz Sadaqat’s journey from Peshawar’s streets to Pakistan’s T20I spotlight. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Maaz Sadaqat could hardly have asked for a more emphatic introduction to international T20 cricket. After scoring a brisk half-century in only his third Pakistan outing, against Sri Lanka, the 21-year-old left-hander followed it with a breathtaking 96 off 51 balls in the second match, helping the national side register their highest men’s T20I total on home soil and clinch the series with an 82-run victory.

The two innings came on the back of a remarkable Caribbean Premier League campaign in which Maaz struck two centuries for Jamaica Kingsmen, including one in the final.

He made 112 off 49 balls in the eliminator before scoring 114 off 58 deliveries in the title decider. Although Jamaica lost the final, his performances had established him as one of the most exciting young batters in the tournament.

His innings against Sri Lanka have now brought that promise to a wider audience. Sunday’s knock featured six fours and seven sixes, taking Pakistan to 215-3 and equalling the record for the most sixes by a Pakistan batter in a men’s T20I innings.

Maaz fell four runs short of a maiden international century, but by then he had already helped Pakistan secure an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match series.

After Maaz’s 96, former Pakistan captain Mohammad Rizwan recalled on social media how the young batter had visited his home in Peshawar as a boy, accompanied by his elder brother, Haroon, with the ambition of one day representing Pakistan.

“It feels like yesterday when a young boy came to meet me in my Peshawar home with his brother Haroon, carrying a dream of one day playing for Pakistan,” Rizwan wrote on X, adding that seeing Maaz in the national shirt had brought him immense happiness.

The message offered a glimpse into the journey behind the sudden international attention, featuring a progression from tape-ball cricket in Peshawar to age-group cricket, domestic competition and, eventually, performances that could no longer be overlooked.

Born in May 2005, Maaz grew up playing cricket on the streets with plastic and tape balls. His elder brother, a first-class cricketer, helped introduce him to organised cricket after he completed his matriculation, taking him to Ashnaghar Cricket Club.

“I was a school kid and was hitting big sixes in my first club cricket game and everyone was super impressed,” Maaz had earlier recalled in a video posted by the Pakistan Cricket Board. His family subsequently encouraged him to attend trials, opening the way into the board’s pathways programme.

He progressed through district and regional under-19 cricket for Peshawar and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, finishing among the leading run-scorers in youth competitions before representing Pakistan at the 2021 Under-19 Asia Cup and the 2022 Under-19 World Cup. The experience gave him an early grounding in competitive cricket, but the transition to senior level would require more than the ability to strike the ball cleanly.

Maaz made his first-class debut for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in the 2022-23 Quaid-e-Azam Trophy. He soon demonstrated that his attacking instincts could translate into the longer format, scoring 91 in one of his early matches. He also gained experience overseas, making his List A debut for City Club in Bangladesh’s Dhaka Premier Division in 2023.

Raffatullah Mohmand, his regional head coach and a former Pakistan player, was among those who helped guide his development. He recommended Maaz for the Bangladesh opportunity after the youngster impressed in Peshawar, believing he deserved greater exposure.

“Apart from being a quick learner and skilled cricketer, Maaz’s success also lies in in-depth preparation of all the challenges fronting him,” Raffatullah had said.

According to the coach, Maaz had begun observing and speaking to experienced players, including Rizwan, Iftikhar Ahmed and current Pakistan Sahibzada Farhan, from his teenage years, applying what he learned from them to his training and preparation. That willingness to learn, Raffatullah suggested, had helped accelerate his progress.

The first major glimpse of Maaz’s potential on a national stage came in the Pakistan Super League in May 2025. Making his debut for Peshawar Zalmi against Islamabad United, he walked in with his side in trouble at 38-3 while chasing 144. Rather than allowing the situation to dictate his approach, he counterattacked, scoring 55 off 33 balls in a match-winning partnership of 102 with Babar Azam.

Babar remained unbeaten on 53, while Sadaqat’s contribution earned him the Player of the Match award. For the young batter, sharing a partnership with one of Pakistan’s leading players was a moment of personal significance.

“With Babar at the other end, I felt no pressure and I turned to my natural game, acquiring more belief,” Maaz had said. “That time also helped me realise how much I have trained all my life to get here and do well.”

The innings appeared to announce the arrival of a promising new talent. Yet the attention it generated soon faded amid the demands of a crowded domestic calendar and the steady competition for places in Pakistan’s white-ball sides.

Maaz’s next breakthrough came later that year at the ACC Men’s Asia Cup Rising Stars in Doha. Representing Pakistan Shaheens in November 2025, he delivered an outstanding all-round campaign that made it difficult for selectors to ignore him.

He began with an unbeaten 96 off 54 balls against Oman and then produced one of the tournament’s defining performances against India ‘A’, taking two wickets for 12 runs before hitting an unbeaten 79 off 47 balls to help Pakistan Shaheens win by eight wickets. He finished as the tournament’s leading run-scorer with 258 runs in five innings at an average of 129, while taking seven wickets. He was named Player of the Tournament.

The performances were significant not simply because of the runs and wickets, but because they showed Maaz’s capacity to influence a match in more than one discipline. His left-arm orthodox spin offered an additional option, while his batting demonstrated that he could attack quality opposition without losing sight of the situation.

The Rising Stars tournament placed him firmly in the conversation around Pakistan’s future white-ball players. His subsequent engagements with Pakistan Shaheens, including overseas tours, provided further experience against different conditions and bowling attacks.

His next PSL campaign, however, was less transformative. Playing for Hyderabad Kingsmen in earlier this year, Maaz featured in 12 matches and scored 260 runs at an average of 23.63 and a strike rate of 178.08.

His highest score was 64, and he registered two half-centuries, hitting 27 fours and 16 sixes. The team reached the final, but Maaz’s season did not produce the same defining headline as his debut for Zalmi or his subsequent performances in the Caribbean.

The numbers nevertheless reflected a batter who continued to score quickly, even if he was not yet converting his starts into the kind of substantial innings that would make him a regular subject of national debate. His challenge remained to marry his high scoring rate with greater consistency.

Maaz had already taken another important step in March 2026, when he made his One-day International debut against Bangladesh.

In the second ODI, he scored 75 off 46 balls and took three wickets for 23 runs, earning the Player of the Match award. He finished the three-match series with 99 runs and three wickets.

The subsequent ODI series against Australia proved more difficult, with Sadaqat managing 35 runs across three matches. His early international record in the format offered encouragement, but it also illustrated the adjustment required to establish himself against senior opposition over a sustained period.

It was in T20 cricket, though, that he would soon make his most emphatic statement representing Jamaica Kingsmen in the CPL.

His selection for Pakistan’s T20I side, however, had a timeline of its own. The PCB announced him in the 15-member squad for the Asian Games in June, months before the CPL campaign. The tournament in Japan, scheduled for September and October, was to provide him with another opportunity to gain international T20 experience. His franchise commitments in the Caribbean meant that he was expected to join the national camp after the CPL concluded.

The Asian Games selection was an indication that the selectors were already monitoring his development. The CPL then offered a compelling demonstration of what he could bring to the format, before even as his international debut came in the Games, in which Pakistan took the silver medal.

While Maaz did not make a big impact in the two games Pakistan played in Japan, he impressed with a 50 off 29 balls as Pakistan chased down a target of 183 to take a 1-0 lead. Two days later, he went further, almost scoring a century.

The back-to-back performances brought together the strands of Sadaqat’s development — the fearless strokeplay first noticed in Peshawar, the lessons absorbed from senior players, the breakthrough in the PSL, the all-round success at the Rising Stars tournament and the proof of his power-hitting in the CPL.

At 21, he offers Pakistan an attacking left-handed batter who can also contribute with slow left-arm spin. His record so far also suggests that the next stage will be about consistency rather than discovery. The challenge is to turn eye-catching innings into a sustained run of performances and establish himself across formats, particularly in one-day cricket.

For now, Rizwan’s recollection of the young visitor to his Peshawar home provides an apt frame for Maaz’s rise. The dream of playing for Pakistan has become reality, and his first two T20Is have ensured that the conversation around him has moved well beyond the domestic circuit. The task ahead is to make this promising beginning last.

item.description:
Bangladesh pushed towards a big win over Afghanistan in the one-off Test after a brilliant century from Litton Das helped them set a target of 479 runs in Abu Dhabi on Monday.

Litton scored 102, his seventh Test hundred, as Bangladesh declared on 372-7 on day four at Sheikh Zayed Cricket Stadium, having achieved a 106-run lead in the first innings.

Afghanistan finished the day on 132-3 with Sediqullah Atal and Hashmatullah Shahidi batting on 35 and 19, respectively.

Bangladesh will expect their pacers and spinners to seal victory on a wearing pitch on Tuesday.

Bangladesh seamer Ebadot Hossain gave his team an early breakthrough when he dismissed Abdul Malik for two in just the second over of the innings.

Hasan Mahmud, who took a hat-trick during his five-wicket haul in the first innings, had Shahidullah Kamal caught behind for 19 before Rahmat Shah and Sediqullah added 82 for the third wicket.

Rahmat, who made a century in Afghanistan’s first innings of 240, compiled a battling 51, hitting five fours and a six, before Ebadot had him caught behind by Litton.

It was Litton’s eighth dismissal behind the stumps in the match, setting a new record for Bangladesh.

The previous best was seven dismissals by Khaled Mashud against Zimbabwe in February 2004.

Earlier, Bangladesh resumed at 223-6 and were indebted to a seventh-wicket stand of 149 between Litton and Mehidy Hasan Miraz, who finished with 52 not out.

Afghanistan were sloppy in the field as they let off Litton on 14, 26 and 67, also missing a run-out chance against Miraz, capping a disappointing day.

Mohammad Saleem, Zia-ur-Rehman and Yamin Ahmadzai took two wickets apiece for Afghanistan.
