item.title: Three years after October 7, global attention on Gaza has receded. The real test will come after Israel’s election. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
This week marks three years since Hamas’ massacre of October 7 , 2023, in which some 1,200 people, most of them Israeli civilians, were killed and 251 taken hostage.
What followed were two years of devastating war waged by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) in Gaza, which a UN commission of inquiry , leading genocide scholars and major human rights organisations have concluded amounted to genocide. Much of the strip lies in ruins and more than 74,000 Palestinians are dead, with thousands more believed to remain buried under the rubble.
A year ago this week, a US-imposed ceasefire was finally forced on both sides -- though mainly on paper. While major IDF assaults have ceased, Israeli attacks in Gaza have continued, in addition to unbridled Jewish settler violence in the West Bank .
Despite this, global attention on Gaza has waned. As the US–Israeli war with Iran began dominating the headlines, earlier pledges by many states to help drive the peace process forward have proved once again wanting, even hollow.
Now, Israel is preparing for a highly polarized parliamentary election on October 27, which could be consequential for the entire region. If a less extreme government takes office, will the world’s attention to Gaza and the West Bank -- and the pressure it has generated -- hold?
What the peace plan delivered, and what it didn’t
The first phase of US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan in Gaza largely succeeded. The remaining living Israeli hostages came home in exchange for close to 2,000 Palestinian prisoners and detainees , and the remains of deceased hostages were returned over the following months. Hundreds of thousands of displaced Gazans moved back to the north. Israeli forces pulled back to a “yellow line”, and the UN Security Council endorsed the plan and a US-chaired “Board of Peace”.
However, the world’s expectations for “all guns to fall silent” were soon dashed. A year after the ceasefire was signed on October 9 , 2025, the Gaza Health Ministry, whose figures the UN uses, reports close to 1,400 Gazans have been killed.
Aid remains restricted, meaningful reconstruction has yet to begin, and another winter is approaching for families living in tents and damaged buildings.
Without sustained international engagement, the second phase of the Trump plan has largely stalled. Hamas has not disarmed. An International Stabilization Force intended to bring security to Gaza has yet to deploy , despite a US commander being appointed in January. And the technocratic Palestinian committee meant to run Gaza has not taken control on the ground.
Only last week did the Board of Peace unveil a six-month, US$2.45 billion plan to begin rebuilding, but this is a fraction of the US$71.4 billion it estimates recovery will require over a decade.
And all of this depends on Hamas surrendering its weapons. Israel will not allow reconstruction before full disarmament, and Hamas will not disarm on the plan’s terms. Reform of the domestically unpopular Palestinian Authority has been slow, and Israel’s right-wing government has been in campaign mode for months, with strong incentives to spoil the progress.
Recognition of Palestine by more than 150 states has not changed the reality on the ground. The international pressure that helped bring about the ceasefire has proved much harder to sustain since the worst of the violence ended.
Attention faded, but did not disappear
Media and public attention to distant atrocities is notoriously short-lived. It peaks with the most extreme violence and quickly subsides once violence becomes chronic, or once another crisis begins to dominate the news.
Gaza has followed part of this script. As mass casualty bombardments gave way to near-daily “lower-intensity” attacks, headlines receded . The US–Israeli war with Iran, which began in late February, absorbed much of the world’s limited attention span . Ukraine and, in short bursts, Lebanon, competed for what remained.
Most people rank foreign crises far below domestic concerns – health care, jobs and the cost of living -- and the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has reached directly into people’s pockets through the price of petrol. Gaza, for most, never did.
A year ago, I warned that once the mass violence in Gaza ended, international attention would wane, making it easier for either side to derail the peace process. That is largely what happened, but not entirely.
What stands out about the past year is less the weakening of attention to Gaza than the extent to which some of it remained. While mass opinion largely moved on, elite opinion (some legislators, officials, commentators) and the smaller but highly committed body of concerned global citizens did not.
The latter drew on a Palestinian solidarity movement built over decades, turning outrage into a sustained global campaign -- though some of their rhetoric and tactics also deepened polarization , at home and in Israel.
Sudan, meanwhile, which the UN has described as the world’s largest humanitarian crisis, shows the flip side . With no equivalent global campaign behind it, it has struggled to hold the world’s gaze.
The invisibility of one crisis and the hyper-visibility of another are two faces of the same problem: which atrocities galvanise public opinion depends less on their severity than on who is organised enough to make us pay attention.
A deepening crisis in the West Bank
The sustained, if narrower, global pressure campaign on Gaza soon had a new source of outrage: settler violence in the West Bank.
The United Nations had recorded an average of six settler attacks on Palestinians a day by June of this year, a pace higher than any year on record. By July , killings linked to settler attacks had exceeded the total for all of 2025. Thousands of Palestinians have also been displaced as settlement expansion has accelerated.
Some European governments had already banned trade with the settlements ; others, such as the United Kingdom, more recently found they could no longer afford to ignore the crisis. In September, London announced its ban , with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accusing “settler terrorists” of ethnic cleansing.
Although the European Union is Israel’s largest trading partner and the UK another important one, the economic impact of these measures will be modest since settlements export relatively little. The significance is mainly political.
Moreover, if the European pressure is meant in part to sway Israeli voters before the election, it’s unclear how effective it will be. Outside pressure before an election tends to rally a leader’s loyal base, and the global outrage over Gaza has already reinforced a siege mentality among many Israeli Jews.
The real external pressure, however, will need to come after the election.
The decisive stick for moving the peace process forward lies in Washington, given how much any Israeli government depends on US support. The main carrot for Israel would be normalization of relations with Saudi Arabia – and with it much of the Arab and Muslim world. But this is a reward Riyadh has tied to a credible path to Palestinian statehood.
Another factor will weigh even more, and it is often underestimated: the Israeli public’s profound need for a sense of security .
Shattered on October 7, this need helps explain how the war in Gaza was fought, though it cannot excuse it -- just as no grievance, whatever its roots, could justify Hamas’ massacre of civilians.
It will now shape how Israelis vote -- and what any new government believes it can risk -- far more than sticks or carrots from abroad.
The harder test: shades of grey
Last year, I argued that meaningful progress in Gaza and the West Bank would require an Israeli government willing to make hard choices.
The October 27 election will be a test of whether one emerges. Polls suggest Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar could become the largest party in the Knesset (Israel’s parliament), but it may struggle to form a governing coalition without the support of Arab-Israeli parties, a prospect Eisenkot has refused to embrace.
A change of government would matter. It could bring a real effort to rein in settler violence, a more cooperative approach to the Board of Peace’s efforts in Gaza, and a state inquiry into the October 7 attacks.
However, it is less likely to bring a fundamental change in policy on Israel’s illegal occupation of the Palestinian territories. Eisenkot has ruled out a Palestinian state for the foreseeable future , and any coalition he leads would probably include right-wing partners.
Herein lies a paradox. Global action is most easily mobilised against clearly villainous actions and actors. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current coalition, including far-right ministers such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, has made the case for international pressure easy.
A more moderate-sounding, centre -right government would make it much harder to sustain. Governments that could not ignore Israel’s conduct under Netanyahu may ease off their pressure. Some media may treat an Eisenkot-led victory as a path towards resolution, and concerned citizens may struggle to keep people’s attention focused on an occupation that grinds on more quietly.
If sustained attention depends on extreme cases, then the quieter periods in between are where policies stall and abuses continue. The past year suggests that outrage alone cannot carry meaningful pressure through those periods.
Three years after October 7, the guns in Gaza are quieter, but far from silent. The question for the year ahead is whether the world keeps listening.
Eyal Mayroz is Senior Lecturer in Peace and Conflict Studies, University of Sydne y. This article previously appeared in the Conversation and has been reprinted under special arrangement.

item.title: No exit: Why Bangladesh's cities keep burning. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For the last fifteen years, buildings have been catching fire for the same reasons, with the same promises following each tragedy. If resilience truly starts at home, then home, in Bangladesh's cities, is precisely where it keeps failing.
Every October 13 , the world observes the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction. This year's theme, "Resilience starts at home," is meant to be read gently, as a call to prepare our households for disasters. In urban Bangladesh, it reads more like a warning.
A city that keeps reliving the same night
The roll call is long and familiar. From the Nimtoli chemical warehouse fire in 2010, which killed at least 124 people, to the Tazreen factory fire in 2012, the Bailey Road restaurant fire in 2024 and the Korail fire in 2025, Bangladesh's cities have repeatedly witnessed preventable loss of life and homes.
Across such incidents, well over 400 people have died. Almost none of the resulting court cases have reached a verdict.
The details differ, but the pattern does not: the conditions that allow a fire to become a disaster are often present long before the first flame.
The disaster is often built before the fire starts
Faulty electrical wiring and overloaded circuits are among the most common triggers. Gas cylinders used in homes, restaurants and vehicles can turn routine activities into deadly emergencies. Chemical warehouses and flammable stock are routinely stored in buildings never designed to contain them, turning a fire into an inferno within minutes.
Factories and high-rise commercial buildings with inadequate or locked emergency exits become death traps when smoke fills a corridor. Restaurants have proliferated on upper floors of buildings not designed for such use, sometimes obstructing escape routes. In informal settlements, tightly packed housing, exposed wiring and narrow lanes can allow a single spark to spread across an entire neighbourhood.
The problem, then, is not simply fire. Risk is built into the way buildings are designed, approved, occupied and maintained.
Rules on paper, risk in practice
Bangladesh is not short of regulation. The Bangladesh National Building Code, mandatory since 2006 and updated in 2020, sets out fire-resistant design, mandatory exits, hydrants, sprinklers and detection systems, and any building must secure fire safety clearance from the Fire Service and Civil Defence before RAJUK approves its design.
The gap is not in the law; it is in its application. A parliamentary disclosure put the share of Dhaka buildings violating the code at around 66 per cent. A RAJUK survey of over 200,000 structures found roughly two-thirds defective, risky or uninhabitable, while separate data found nine in ten surveyed buildings deviated from their approved designs. Too often, a design approved on paper is altered or repurposed in practice, without effective follow-up.
From certificates to inspections that bite
Closing this gap does not require new laws so much as the will to enforce existing ones. Building and fire approvals need to be digitised and linked, so a change of use or an expired licence is visible to regulators automatically rather than discovered after a tragedy.
Fire clearance should not be a one-time certificate issued at construction; it needs to be a recurring inspection, with real penalties, including sealing premises, for buildings that let it lapse. The Bangladesh Building Regulatory Authority envisaged under the BNBC 2020 should be operationalised with a clear mandate for consistent enforcement. RAJUK, city corporations and the Fire Service need enough trained inspectors to visit the hundreds of thousands of buildings under their jurisdiction. And court cases following major fires need to reach a verdict.
Six policy fixes we cannot keep postponing
Planners, engineers, lawyers and fire-safety experts have converged on broadly the same list of reforms after each tragedy; what has been missing is follow-through.
First , establish a dedicated Building Regulatory Authority to implement the Building Code consistently, instead of leaving it split across RAJUK, city corporations and the Fire Service with no single body accountable.
Second , harmoni z e the Fire Prevention and Extinction Act 2003 with the Building Code, so the two frameworks set the same standard.
Third , publish a tiered public registry of high- and moderate-risk buildings, so tenants and regulators know which structures need urgent attention before they burn.
Fourth , require every building to display an annually renewable occupancy and fire safety certificate at its entrance.
Fifth , make hospital, industrial and commercial fire protocols mandatory: functioning lifts, unlocked and clearly marked exits, refuge floors and regular evacuation drills.
Sixth , back all of this with real investment in the Fire Service's staffing and equipment, alongside a coordinated national occupational safety framework of the kind the International Labour Organization has urged Bangladesh to adopt since the Bailey Road incident.
Resilience starts at home, or it does not start at all
Every fire on this list was, in hindsight, foreseeable: a blocked exit, a warehouse in the wrong place, a licence never renewed. Resilience starting at home means exactly that literal thing here -- a safe electrical line, a clear staircase, a landlord who does not store chemicals beneath a family's bedroom.
Government agencies can write codes and NGOs can rebuild what fire destroys, but neither can retrofit safety into a building after the fact. Bangladesh's cities do not lack rules; they lack the follow-through to make those rules real, in every home, before the next spark catches.
Khondoker Golam Tawhid is the Programme Head of the Disaster Risk Management Programme at BRAC .

item.title: 'Riyadh no longer feels safe': Houthi strikes shatter Saudi capital's aura of calm. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
'Riyadh no longer feels safe': Houthi strikes shatter Saudi capital's aura of calm

Submitted by Faisal Edroos on Mon, 10/12/2026 - 16:25
Deadly attacks on the kingdom's main airport have shaken expatriates' sense of security and threatened Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to become a global hub for tourism and investment
Smoke and flames rise from King Khalid Airport in Riyadh on 10 October 2026 after Yemen's Houthis attacked the facility (Reuters)
Off

Riyadh has long presented itself as a safe haven from the turmoil engulfing the Middle East.

But deadly Houthi strikes on the Saudi capital's main airport have shattered that sense of security, leaving expatriate families questioning whether they can continue to build their lives in the kingdom.

At least 12 people were killed and more than 300 injured when Yemen's Houthis attacked the King Khalid International Airport on Saturday.

The movement, which also fired cruise missiles at oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, said the attacks were in response to Riyadh's support for government forces in Yemen's civil war and a Saudi air strike on Sanaa airport earlier this year.

CCTV footage aired by state broadcaster Al Ekhbariya showed pilgrims dressed in white, waiting to travel to Mecca for Umrah, scrambling for safety as dust filled an airport lounge and ceiling panels fell to the floor.

Among the dead were a Bangladeshi cleric, a Syrian mother of four and a US citizen.

A second strike the following day killed one person and injured at least 11 others.

 
 
 
 
View this post on Instagram
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

A post shared by Middle East Eye (@middleeasteye)

"Pilgrims should never have to fear for their lives while travelling on a religious journey," Bilal, a 39-year-old British national who has lived in the capital for at least seven years, told Middle East Eye.

"There's no way the Houthis can spin this. There's no justifying attacks on ordinary people, and no way they can defend striking a civilian facility - whatever the Saudi-led coalition did in the war years ago."

Beyond the immediate carnage, the attacks struck at the heart of the kingdom's carefully cultivated image as a secure destination for international business, tourism and investment.

'There's no justifying attacks on ordinary people, and no way they [the Houthis] can defend striking a civilian facility - whatever the Saudi-led coalition did in the war years ago'

- Bilal, British expat

On Sunday, a major energy conference drew only a handful of delegates and with the kingdom's flagship business event, the Future Investment Initiative, just two weeks away, the attacks have raised questions about Riyadh's ability to project an image of stability.

Bilal told MEE that while he would find it difficult to give up his well-paid job and comfortable life in the kingdom, the scale and frequency of the attacks had prompted some expatriate families to question whether civilian spaces were safe.

"I have no intention of returning to the UK. My family and I have made a life here. But would I consider sending them back if the situation spiralled and there were more frequent attacks? Absolutely."

Mohamed, a British national who has lived in Riyadh on and off for the past decade, said while he also considered the kingdom a safe place to raise his family, he was unsettled by the failure of missile interceptors to protect the airport, one of the kingdom's most important transport hubs.

"My children are also pretty scared by what's happening," he told MEE.

"I've reassured them that they will be safe, but with schools being cancelled and some foreigners openly expressing their plans to return to their home countries, it's becoming much harder to explain

"Riyadh no longer feels safe."

Vulnerable economic ambitions

The attacks mark a dangerous escalation in Saudi Arabia's confrontation with Yemen's Houthis, who control much of the country's north.

The conflict was largely locked in a stalemate until Saudi-led forces struck Sanaa airport in July, seeking to prevent an aircraft carrying Houthi officials from Iran from landing in the rebel-held capital.

The Houthis responded by threatening to impose a reciprocal blockade, vowing to target Saudi interests in response to restrictions on their own access to the airspace and transport networks they rely on.

They subsequently declared an embargo on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, an increasingly important alternative route for the kingdom's oil exports after the Iran war disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

The latest escalation is rooted in hostilities that began in 2014, when the Houthis capitalised on widespread discontent over fuel subsidy cuts and the failure of a UN-sponsored national dialogue to resolve Yemen's deep political and economic divisions.

After rejecting proposals for a new federal structure, the Iran-aligned movement advanced south and seized the capital, Sanaa, forcing President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi's government into retreat.

The Houthis' advance prompted a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015, launching a military campaign aimed at restoring the internationally recognised government.

Armed with US-made bombs and British-made fighter jets, Saudi Arabia and its allies launched a devastating war that killed hundreds of thousands of people, many of them through hunger, disease and the collapse of essential services.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who spearheaded the kingdom's war effort in 2015, has since sought to transform Saudi Arabia into a destination for foreign investment, international conferences, entertainment and tourism.

But the Houthi attacks, alongside Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz - through which roughly a fifth of global oil and gas supplies normally pass - have exposed the vulnerability of those ambitions to regional conflict.

Growing tensions

The crisis has also exposed growing tensions between Gulf states and Washington.

For decades, Bahrain, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Oman either hosted US military bases, infrastructure or access, and spent heavily on American weapons and technology. 

In return, Washington served as the region's principal military partner and security guarantor.

But a Gulf analyst, who requested anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, said the relationship was under severe strain.

'Trump can't tell Saudi Arabia it's on its own and expect the kingdom to accept that as a serious security guarantee'

- Gulf analyst

The kingdom was already concerned by US President Donald Trump's decision to abandon diplomacy in favour of war with Iran, the analyst said, leaving regional allies to bear the consequences of a conflict they had not chosen.

Trump's response to the attacks on Riyadh deepened that frustration after he said Saudi Arabia was "able to defend" itself.

The uncertainty has increased the significance of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan in August.

The pact is intended to strengthen collective deterrence, although the timing and scale of any Turkish troop deployment remain uncertain as Ankara considers its next steps.

"Trump can't tell Saudi Arabia it's on its own and expect the kingdom to accept that as a serious security guarantee," the analyst said.

"The US has spent decades asking Gulf states to invest in American weapons and build their security around Washington. When the threat materialises, dismissing it as something Saudi Arabia can handle raises serious questions about what that partnership is actually worth."

UK advises against using any Saudi airport except Medina

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Mon, 10/12/2026 - 09:12
The UK has further warned British nationals not to try and leave Saudi Arabia via airports in the country
An air traffic control tower is seen at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on 19 September 2026 (AFP)
Off

The British government has advised its citizens against all but essential travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including Jeddah and Dammam, and to all airports in the country except Medina International Airport. 

The UK has further warned British nationals not to try and leave Saudi Arabia via airports in the country.

This comes after a fresh attack on a passenger terminal at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, which killed at least one person and wounded 11.

Saturday's attack on the airport killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 - making it the deadliest strike on a Gulf country since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on 28 February.

Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed in the attack. 

It was the third attack on the airport in a week, following earlier strikes that killed four people and damaged a Saudi commercial aircraft.

The British Foreign Office updated its official guidance on Sunday to advise UK nationals against "all but essential travel to all airports within Saudi Arabia except for Medina International Airport", as well as "all but essential travel to Aseer province, Riyadh province, Najran province, Jizan province and the cities of Taif, Jeddah and Dammam".

Houthi forces warn against use of Saudi airports following Riyadh attack
Read More »

The Foreign Office further advised against all travel to within 10km of the border with Yemen.

"As an alternative to airports within Saudi Arabia," the Foreign Office said British nationals wishing to depart Saudi Arabia should consider options to travel by land to neighbouring countries and fly from there.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree warned travellers, airlines and shipping companies not to use Saudi airports and airspace, saying they are “exposed to targeting and a theatre for operations by our forces”, with the exception of the airports of Mecca and Medina.

Saree said Houthi forces carried out several operations against King Khalid airport on Saturday, “resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the airport and its complete closure”.

He also listed King Fahd Airport in Dammam, an Aramco-affiliated petrol station and a refinery in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Region among the targets.

'Dangerous escalation'

The latest attacks mark a significant escalation in the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi movement in Yemen, with renewed fighting and a Saudi-led military offensive against the group. 

British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting condemned Saturday's airport attack as a "dangerous escalation" and "completely contemptible action".

Meanwhile in Yemen, air strikes have been reported on the Hamdan district in Sanaa and two more strikes on al-Zurbi Road in the Hayfan district in Taiz, according to Sanaa-based media. 

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activate Mecca Pact amid war with Houthis
Read More »

Missile attacks were also reported on the border district of al-Dhaher in Saada province. No casualties have been reported so far. 

The US State Department has urged American citizens to take "extreme caution" when travelling through airports in Saudi Arabia, amid renewed attacks.

"U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization to use the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, as well as the airports in Jeddah and Dammam," its official account on X said.

"Please take extreme caution when using all major airports in Saudi Arabia. U.S. citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."

Amid the escalation, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke over the phone to his Saudi counterpart Faisal bin Farhan.

According to Iranian state media, Araghchi said Iran was ready to help start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen. 

He expressed concern over escalating tensions, and insisted that a "military approach and ignoring a political solution will further complicate the current situation".

Araghchi also further stressed that crisis in the region "have no military solution", adding that Tehran is "ready to provide any assistance to help start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen and to help achieve a political solution".

item.description:
Dhaka woke up on Sunday to an Air Quality Index reading of 167, which the index classifies as "unhealthy."
Dhaka has long been among the most polluted cities in the world, and yet, with winter fast approaching and the imminent threat of air that is simply not fit to breathe, we continue to do little to address it.
The causes are no mystery: Brick kilns on the city's fringes, many operating with little regard for the rules; construction sites that leave sand and debris uncovered; roads dug up and rebuilt in a never-ending cycle; and a clogged, fume-spewing traffic system.
What remains missing is the will to act on them. Every year, the authorities announce drives, fines, and demolitions, and every year, the air gets no cleaner. Such efforts begin loudly, fade quietly, and return only when the numbers make headlines again.
Pollution control cannot be a seasonal activity, any more than breathing is.
The cost, meanwhile, is being paid by ordinary people. The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution kills around seven million people worldwide each year, mostly through stroke, heart disease, lung cancer, and respiratory infections.
For those in Dhaka, where millions are outdoors at all times, those figures show up in crowded hospital corridors, missed school days, and lost income.
By now, there are no secrets to solutions: From construction sites needing to follow dust control rules, to brick kilns needing to be regulated, to accelerating cleaner energy and technologies that already exist.
Clean air should never be viewed as a luxury nor a favour. It is something every citizen is owed. A city that cannot guarantee it has failed at the most basic test of governance.
We should not wait for the smog to thicken before we remember that. The time to act is now, while we can still breathe.

item.title: Fixing our banking sector. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Reports that the International Monetary Fund will likely press for strict, time-bound deadlines to fix weak banks and reduce the astronomical non-performing loans (NPLs) we have racked up should serve as a wake-up call for our leaders.
Despite dreams of self-sufficiency, the reality we must contend with is that, at present, our economic delegations are preparing to negotiate a fresh financial package with international lenders.
To that end, it is also abundantly clear that if we are to continue to receive the financial assistance our economy needs, Bangladesh can no longer afford half-measures in reforming what can safely be referred to as its crippled banking sector.
Decades of political patronage, reckless default cultures, and opaque loan write-offs have brought our financial architecture to the brink. As such, we simply no longer have the option to treat bank reform as an optional administrative exercise.
The rot in our financial system is neither hidden nor new. For years, massive amounts of liquidity have been siphoned off through fraud, insider lending, and willful defaults, leaving state-owned and private commercial banks saddled with staggering piles of debt.
It goes without saying that a banking sector choking on defaulted loans cannot be of help to the economy, thereby stunting our growth and deepening the broader fiscal crisis.
While no nation likes external pressure, we would do well to not view it as an infringement on sovereignty, but rather as a catalyst for accountability.
Financial stability is the backbone of national security and economic survival, and it is a shame that Bangladesh has not experienced it for some time now, if ever.
If setting strict deadlines is what is needed to cleanse our balance sheets and end the culture of loan default, then so be it. We must do what we can to restore public trust and build a modern, transparent banking system.

item.title: War and peace. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On the evening of February 24, 2022, I was due to teach an internal medicine session to a group of junior colleagues, among them a young physician from Ukraine.
She could not speak through her tears, and could not attend. Russian tanks had crossed her country's border hours earlier. I remember the silence on that call more clearly than almost anything said in it.
On the morning of October 7, 2023, I woke early and watched, in something close to real time, young people being dragged away from a music festival in southern Israel, and the destruction, within hours, of the Israeli villages bordering Gaza. Within perhaps half a day, hundreds were dead.
In the months since October 7, 2023, I have watched, night after night, as Gaza was reduced to rubble, hospitals bombed to ashes, and aid workers killed while children ran toward soup kitchens holding out bent and broken utensils, while white-painted drones circled overhead and IDF mortars piercing the sky above the blue Mediterranean.
And this year, a third conflict opened before I had recovered from the second: Iran and the United States, missiles fired across the Gulf, Saudi Arabia itself struck by Iranian fire meant for someone else.
Three theatres. Three of the most technologically advanced militaries in human history, deploying precision munitions, autonomous drones, and missile-defense systems worth billions of dollars.
And the result, in every case, is not zero. It is sub-zero.
More dead than before the shooting started. No peace concluded. No side visibly deterred.
Gaza in ruins. Ukraine still waiting for an end no one can date. The Gulf still bracing for the war's next act.
I have carried this fear since I was young enough to watch the towers fall in New York in 2001 -- nearly live, on the BBC, in the hospital corridor where I was on duty.
A nurse burst through the door, breathless, calling out my name twice -- “Rajani! Rajani!” -- as though the news itself could not wait for a full sentence. Some planes, she said, had struck the roof of a tower in New York.
Even Swedish radio, usually so measured, could not yet decipher what was happening, and for a long moment neither could we, standing together in that corridor, disbelieving.
And the tragic aftermath of nearly two decades of war that followed -- in Iraq, Syria, and Afghanistan -- still haunts a generation of women denied their schooling, wrapped head to foot in black, in Kabul and elsewhere, in what was once a more modern country.
Weeks, months later, came a similar news alert: Netanyahu had ordered civilians in southern Lebanon to flee before a bombing spree. That same evening, sharing this over dinner with a friend, I found myself asking aloud what would happen if Putin attacked Sweden and told us to flee.
Flee where? For one unsettling moment, I did not want to know whether I was Lebanese, or Swedish, or a Bengali. I was simply a disposable object, waiting to be thrown into the trash of human folly.
And where does the Iran-US war fit into this -- a war still ongoing, its fragile ceasefires broken. I think here of a friend's son, married to an Iranian physician. On at least two occasions, she has flown to Sweden from elsewhere in the EU -- and each time, within days, as though summoned by some cruel and uncanny clock, a new round of bombing has broken out between the US and Iran.
I have joked with her, half-seriously by now: Whenever you are in Sweden, the US bombs Iran. But behind the joke sits something that is not funny at all -- her parents, still in Tehran, waiting out each night not knowing whether the next siren is the one that finally reaches them. Safe, so far. Only so far.
High technology has changed how efficiently human beings can kill one another. It has not changed why we do it, and it has not once, in any of these three wars, produced the thing weapons are supposedly for: Peace.
On August 7, 2026, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement in the city for which it is named -- a pact declaring that an armed attack on any one signatory will be treated as an attack on all three.
Commentators have already nicknamed it a “Sunni NATO,” though it has none of NATO's command structure, and its own foreign ministers insist it targets no one.
It was born, transparently, from the last 18 months: Saudi Arabia absorbing Iranian missile fire, Gulf states losing confidence that Washington will backstop their security in real time.
What concerns me is not the pact itself -- sovereign nations may organize their own defense as they judge wisest.
What concerns me is what comes next. Bangladeshi officials have confirmed that Saudi Arabia has invited Dhaka to consider joining. A junior foreign minister has called the idea something Bangladesh “views positively.” Nothing is decided. But the invitation is real, and so is the danger it opens.
Bangladesh has no quarrel with Iran. It has no stake in the Gulf. But under a mutual-defense clause, an attack on any member becomes everyone's war -- and Bangladesh's two nearest neighbours are nuclear-armed and have fought each other four times since 1947. The Radcliffe Line still runs raw through this region's memory.
Let me say plainly what I am not saying, because in this country, a byline is often read before an argument is. My surname will be filed by some readers, reflexively, as Hindu, and from there as pro-Indian -- a conflation as old and as unjust as the Radcliffe Line itself.
I write none of this out of sympathy for India over Pakistan, or Pakistan over India. I do not want Bangladesh dragged into a war against India, and I do not want it dragged into a war against Iran on Saudi Arabia's behalf, for exactly the same reason: I am against every war, everywhere, without exception, and I do not believe any Bangladeshi, of any faith, gains anything from a grave.
I say this as someone whose mother still lives in Dhaka, and who has, by his own choice, become something other than only Bangladeshi. Sweden is my home now.
I have watched Gaza's children, Tehran's children, and Ukraine's children -- and a Ukrainian doctor unable to speak through her tears -- with the same grief, because I claim no side except the side of those who did not choose any of it.
If Bangladesh is pulled into a war between India and Pakistan or over a Gulf dispute it never chose, the only outcome will be death -- Bangladeshi death, achieving nothing for Bangladesh.
There is a class of victims in these wars that rarely makes the front page, and I have not been able to stop thinking about them.
When the fighting between Iran and the United States widened into the Gulf this year, I watched footage of a drone strike setting fire to fuel tanks near Dubai International Airport -- an airport I have passed through so many times on my way to Dhaka or elsewhere that I could not, at first, quite believe what I was seeing.
What frightened me most, though, was not the airport. It was the millions of people from Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and India who live and work across the Gulf states -- the drivers, nurses, construction workers, and domestic staff whose labour keeps those economies running, and whose remittances keep millions of families afloat back home.
Human rights organizations have already confirmed that Bangladeshi, Pakistani, and Nepali workers were killed in strikes on Gulf cities during this war -- a driver, a security guard, a water-tanker operator, ordinary people who chose this war no more than the residents of Gaza or Kharkiv did. In fact, two Bangladeshis were killed in the recent attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on October 10.
Had the fighting widened rather than paused, the danger to those workers would not have been only physical. It would also have been the danger of unemployment overnight -- a war turning millions of already vulnerable labourers into returnees with no income and no plan, in economies that cannot easily absorb them.
That fear sat in me with exactly the same weight as watching Gaza's children run toward a soup kitchen. A migrant worker killed in Dubai and a starving child in Gaza are not different categories of grief. They are the same failure, wearing different clothes.
Even the world's richest and most powerful nation cannot make the arithmetic of modern weaponry work.
A single Patriot interceptor takes years to build. The United States, still the strongest military and economic power on Earth, is nonetheless carrying a national debt now near forty trillion dollars, growing by billions of dollars every single day.
If a country of that wealth and scale cannot spend its way to peace through weapons, what should a country like Bangladesh conclude?
And this is not a hypothetical question for Bangladesh. Dhaka has recently advanced a deal to buy up to two dozen Chinese J-10CE fighter jets, at a cost reported near $2bn -- one of the largest defense procurements in the country's history.
Reasonable people can debate whether Bangladesh needs to modernize its air force. Probably it does. But before any such sum is committed, its politicians owe the public more than a single moment's reflection. They owe it a dozen.
What could two billion dollars buy in hospitals, schools, flood defenses, for a country that still struggles to fund all three?
Every taka spent on a fighter jet is a taka that cannot feed a child, treat a patient, or build a seawall against the rising water that will, with rising certainty, arrive before any invading army does.
This is the part of the ledger the war planners never show. Every high-tech weapon is a bet that violence, or the credible threat of it, will purchase something -- territory, deterrence, security, victory.
Three live wars, watched in real time by the whole world, have now tested that bet at unprecedented scale and technological sophistication. In every case, the bet has lost. Not broken even. Lost. No child's death has ever repaired a balance sheet. No missile fired has ever paid down a debt.
I write none of this from resentment toward the United States. I say this as a physician whose own career would not exist in its present form without America -- its conferences, its training programs, its medical journals and universities, the sheer excellence of its scientific culture.
I admire it, unreservedly, and I want it strong. That is exactly why watching its finances stretched thin by war, and its own missile stockpiles too depleted to properly defend an ally, causes me grief rather than any satisfaction.
A country I admire should not have to choose between its own future and one more interceptor.
I once spent six months working in Riyadh, and I still remember flying in and out of that city, looking down at a skyline that had not existed within living memory, and wondering, honestly, how it had been built.
Decades earlier, as a PhD student, I had discussed something similar with younger Swedish colleagues -- what people then called the postwar Western miracle: How ruined economies had rebuilt themselves not through conquest but through trade, institutions, and the free movement of people, capital, and ideas.
What I saw from the air over Riyadh, and later over Doha and Dubai, struck me as a second version of the same miracle: Glass towers and universities and airports risen from the desert within two generations, built by planning and investment rather than war.
Whatever one thinks of how that wealth arrived, its existence is a genuine human achievement -- proof that peace, prosperity, human mobility, and the free flow of capital and information are what progress actually looks like, in the Gulf as much as in the West.
None of it was built by weapons. All of it is now, in different ways, being asked to live under weapons' shadow.
That is the deeper waste: Not merely the money spent on armaments, but the fact that it is being subtracted from precisely the kinds of projects -- scientific, medical, economic, civic -- that have actually made nations great.
As a physician, I cannot stop thinking of it in those terms: Every fighter jet and every interceptor is money that did not go toward cancer research, or the next Ebola outbreak, or the next pandemic we have not yet named.
We know, because we have watched it happen twice in this decade already, that we are not owed advance warning.
If there is a lesson buried in seventy years of failed deterrence, it is not military. It is political.
The only durable peace project of the modern era is the European Union -- a continent that fought itself to exhaustion twice in 30 years, and has not fought itself once since 1945.
As a result, a Dane can breakfast in Copenhagen, lunch in Vienna, and dine in Paris, crossing what used to be the most contested borders on Earth without a checkpoint in sight today.
No missile shield built that. Shared institutions did -- habits of coexistence, patiently assembled, chosen over and over rather than imposed once.
South Asia has never had its Schuman moment -- the 1950 declaration that first bound France’s and Germany’s coal and steel industries together and became the seed from which the European Union grew.
It should not need a war to go looking for one. But it could still choose, deliberately, to become the region that tried.
Rajani K Saha writes from Sweden and is a practising physician.
